:::{#def-eigenvalue}
#### Eigenvalue and eigenvector

Let $\matr{A}$ be a $p \times p$ matrix.
A number $\lambda$ is an **eigenvalue** of $\matr{A}$,
and a vector $\vecf{v} \neq \vzero$ of length $p$
is an **eigenvector** of $\matr{A}$ for $\lambda$, if

$$
\underbrace{\matr{A}}_{p \times p}\,\underbrace{\vecf{v}}_{p \times 1}
= \lambda\,\underbrace{\vecf{v}}_{p \times 1}
$$

:::

::: notes
Multiplying by $\matr{A}$ rescales an eigenvector by $\lambda$
and does not change the line it lies on.
Any nonzero multiple $c\,\vecf{v}$ of an eigenvector
is also an eigenvector for the same $\lambda$,
because $\matr{A}(c\,\vecf{v}) = c\,\matr{A}\vecf{v} = c\,\lambda\vecf{v} = \lambda\,(c\,\vecf{v})$.
Some real matrices, such as a rotation by $90$ degrees,
have no real eigenvalues;
their eigenvalues are complex numbers
[@banerjee2014linear, Chapter 11, Example 11.2 and Definition 11.1, pp. 312-313].
:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#exm-eigenvalue}
#### Eigenvectors of a $2 \times 2$ matrix

Let $\matr{A} = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 \end{bmatrix}$.

$(1, 1)$ is an eigenvector for the eigenvalue $3$:

$$
\ba
\begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 \end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}
&= \begin{bmatrix} 2 + 1 \\ 1 + 2 \end{bmatrix}
&& \text{(definition of matrix-vector multiplication)}
\\
&= 3 \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}
&& \text{(factor out } 3 \text{)}
\ea
$$

$(1, -1)$ is an eigenvector for the eigenvalue $1$:

$$
\ba
\begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 \end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ -1 \end{bmatrix}
&= \begin{bmatrix} 2 - 1 \\ 1 - 2 \end{bmatrix}
&& \text{(definition of matrix-vector multiplication)}
\\
&= 1 \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ -1 \end{bmatrix}
&& \text{(factor out } 1 \text{)}
\ea
$$

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#exm-not-eigenvector}
#### A vector that is not an eigenvector

For the same $\matr{A}$,
$(1, 0)$ is not an eigenvector:

$$
\begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 \end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix}
= \begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix},
$$

and no number $\lambda$ gives $(2, 1) = \lambda\,(1, 0)$,
because the second entries would need $1 = \lambda \cd 0$.

:::
